encounters.cc: Progressive difficulty walking and proximal muscle weakness over two years

lines: Progressive difficulty walking and proximal muscle weakness over two years
The patient presents to the Neurology clinic four months following hospitalization for cholesterol embolism syndrome after elective endovascular aneurysm repair.
He reports that it began as a subtle heaviness in his thighs while climbing stairs but has gradually worsened.
Now, he struggles to get up from low chairs and often drops objects when reaching overhead or gripping tools.
He denies pain, numbness, or fasciculations.
There is no history of trauma, infection, or new medications.
- History of mild ischemic stroke (fully recovered)
He has well-controlled hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus.
- Elective endovascular abdominal aortic aneurysm repair (EVAR)
- Warfarin 5 mg PO daily (adjusted per INR)
- Father: Deceased at age 72 from ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm
- Mother: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, age-related macular degeneration
Smoking: Former smoker, 40 pack-year history, quit 5 years ago following mild cerebrovascular event.
Alcohol: Social, typically one glass of red wine with dinner most evenings.
On neurologic examination, he has mild atrophy of the quadriceps and forearm flexors.
Strength testing reveals weakness in both proximal and distal muscle groups in the upper and lower extremities.
Sensation to light touch, vibration, and proprioception is intact.
Laboratory studies show normal creatine kinase, electrolytes, and thyroid function.
The patient undergoes a muscle biopsy for further evaluation.
Microscopic examination of muscle tissue reveals scattered basophilic vacuoles bordered by granular material within the myofibers.
